analysis.one_liner: Raises FDIC insurance to $100 million per business account and eases acquisition of failing banks.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a single committee hearing: introduced with zero cosponsors, it died in the Senate Banking Committee before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after the spring 2023 regional bank failures, this bill would have raised FDIC deposit insurance from $250,000 to $100 million for noninterest-bearing business accounts for two years, doubled the cap on reciprocal deposits, let the FDIC shield uninsured depositors at very large failed banks, and opened a 90-day window in which bank holding companies could buy banks whose stock had fallen 20% or more without regulator approval or antitrust review. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, received one hearing in June 2023, and never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Large businesses and wealthy depositors holding more than $250,000 in noninterest-bearing payroll or treasury accounts would gain $100 million in federally backed insurance. Large bank holding companies would gain a 90-day window to acquire weakened banks without merger approval or antitrust review. Regional banks that use reciprocal deposit networks would gain doubled room to hold large deposits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large corporate depositors and big bank holding companies

how_it_helps.text: Insures up to $100 million per depositor in noninterest-bearing transaction accounts for two years, up from the standard $250,000 limit [S3].

Doubles the reciprocal deposit limit from $5 billion to $10 billion and raises the share of deposits that can be structured this way from 20% to 25%, letting more banks spread large deposits across a network to keep them insured [S3].

Lets the FDIC facilitate mergers or sales of failed banks with $100 billion or more in assets by counting 'non-systemic secondary costs' in its least-cost calculation, effectively making it easier to protect uninsured depositors at large failures [S2, S3].

Waives bank merger approval requirements and the Clayton Act premerger waiting period for 90 days so bank holding companies can acquire banks whose stock has fallen at least 20% since March 1, 2023 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The FDIC Deposit Insurance Fund would bear the cost of the expanded $100 million guarantee, ultimately paid by insured banks through assessments and passed on to bank customers. Communities and competition would bear the cost of faster banking consolidation.
analysis.who_pays_short: The deposit insurance fund and bank customers

drawbacks.text: Guaranteeing $100 million accounts mainly protects large corporate cash, not household savings; the standard limit already covers virtually all individual depositors, so the expanded guarantee functions as a subsidy for big depositors funded through the insurance fund [S3].

The 90-day waiver of merger approvals and the antitrust premerger review for acquisitions of banks whose stock fell 20% or more since March 1, 2023 would speed consolidation of the banking system into larger holding companies [S3].

The adjusted least-cost resolution provision weakens the rule that normally requires the FDIC to choose the method that costs the insurance fund the least, making it easier to rescue uninsured depositors at very large banks [S2, S3].

Banks with less than $250 billion in assets could opt out of the expanded guarantee and be shielded from the related fee, leaving larger institutions to carry the cost and raising fairness questions across the industry [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine purpose—preventing runs on healthy banks by guaranteeing business payroll and operating accounts—could have helped workers whose employers bank at a failing institution. But the design points the largest benefit at the largest depositors, and the acquisition window with its antitrust exemption would have concentrated the banking sector at the very moment weakened banks were most vulnerable. The opt-out for banks under $250 billion and the GAO review requirement temper the design but do not change who gains most.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee after one hearing in June 2023 and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 11, 2023, two months after the spring regional bank failures; its definition of a 'distressed' bank as one whose stock fell 20% or more since March 1, 2023 ties it directly to that episode [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the day it was introduced [S5].
The committee held one hearing on June 22, 2023, printed as S.Hrg. 118-453, and took no further action on the bill [S5].
No senator cosponsored the bill, including none from the sponsor's own party [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still in committee and no vote ever taken in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, deposit insurance stayed at its standard $250,000 limit and merger approvals and antitrust review stayed as they were—so bank customers who would fund expanded assessments and the competitive banking landscape came out relatively better off. The large corporate depositors who sought a $100 million guarantee and the holding companies that sought an approval-free acquisition window gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bank customers and the existing deposit insurance system

for.name: Sen. Bill Hagerty
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Banking Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on June 22, 2023, then took no further action—no markup, no vote—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors—not even from the sponsor's own party's 49 Senate Republicans—so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.note: The $100 million guarantee on noninterest-bearing accounts protects corporate payroll and treasury cash far beyond the $250,000 standard limit that already covers nearly all households, with the cost carried by the insurance fund. Ordinary depositors would see little direct benefit.

A 90-day window would let them acquire banks whose stock had fallen 20% or more without Fed merger approval and with no antitrust premerger filing, accelerating consolidation of banking into fewer, bigger companies.

Doubling the reciprocal deposit cap to $10 billion helps smaller banks compete for large deposits, but they would share the industry-wide assessment burden for the expanded guarantee; banks under $250 billion in assets could opt out of the guarantee itself.

The fund would stand behind up to $100 million per business account and a looser least-cost standard for large-bank resolutions, raising its exposure and the assessments banks pay, which are typically passed to customers.
